newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-OPINION-Inside Canberra-Howard on unilateral free trade.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-OPINION-Inside Canberra-Howard on unilateral free trade.

text.p: The Wets in the government were intrigued by a comment John Howard made last month to the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum energy ministers meeting in Sydney.

Howard said he was looking forward to attending the November meeting in the Philippines of APEC leaders where the leaders would reaffirm the commitment to achieving the Bogor and Osaka goals of free trade and investment by 2020.
Then he added: "All of the economists tell us that trade liberalisation in any country is good for economic growth in that country no matter what other countries do."
"But all governments, and the ministers among us tonight will know this only too well, know the political pressure against liberalisation which can entail significant dislocation in the short term."
"Even business can sometimes speak with two voices on the opening up of markets."
"APEC can help make the benefits of liberalisation clearer by balancing the pain of domestic structural adjustment against the gains from better access to export markets."
It was not the clear-cut statement which industry would like to see from Howard: that there would be no further tariff reductions unless they are matched by market access by our APEC partners.
But at least Howard seemed to be showing some scepticism about the practicality of the doctrine of driving tariffs down to zero no matter what other countries do.

It is worth recalling what Howard, as Opposition Leader said to the annual dinner of the Federal Chamber of Automotive Industries last year: "The proposition that Australia might find herself to be some kind of theoretical martyr to the goal of APEC without having obtained in return responses from countries of that region, is not something that commends itself to me."

APEC groups Australia, Brunei, Canada, Chile, China, Hong Kong, Indonesia, Japan, South Korea, Malaysia, Mexico, New Zealand, Papua New Guinea, the Philippines, Singapore, Taiwan, Thailand, and the United States.
(Views are those of Inside Canberra, not Reuters)
